background_notes.fact: For real a, the complex-valued function f_a(s)=exp(-i*a*s) on the real line is smooth, f_a'(s)=-i*a*f_a(s), |f_a(s)|=1, f_0(s)=1, and f_a(s)f_b(s)=f_(a+b)(s) for real b. For real r,s, |f_a(s)-f_a(r)|<=|a|*|s-r|. Consequently h(s)=f_alpha(s)-Mavg_tau(f_alpha) is smooth and |h'(s)|=|alpha|.

background_notes.justification: The usual complex exponential addition law and exp(it)=cos(t)+i*sin(t) give the product identity, the zero phase and unit modulus for real t. Differentiating the exponential gives the displayed derivative, hence smoothness. Apply the real-variable fundamental theorem of calculus componentwise between r and s and bound the norm of the integral by the integral of |a| to obtain the phase difference bound. Subtracting a constant leaves the derivative unchanged. These are routine exponential calculus properties at the functions actually used, not an assumed covariance estimate.

background_notes.fact: A continuous complex function on [0,tau], tau>0, is integrable componentwise; its integral is linear, the integral of a constant c is tau*c, and |integral g|<=integral |g|. Integration preserves pointwise inequalities between continuous real functions. In particular, for continuous f and s in [0,tau], f(s)-Mavg_tau(f)=tau^(-1) integral_0^tau (f(s)-f(r))dr and its modulus is at most tau^(-1) integral_0^tau |f(s)-f(r)|dr.

background_notes.justification: Continuous real and imaginary parts are integrable on the compact interval. Linearity and the constant integral formula give the centered-average identity. For the norm inequality, when I=integral g is nonzero, multiply g by conjugate(I)/|I| and take the real part: |I|=integral Re(conjugate(I)*g/|I|)<=integral |g|; when I=0 the inequality is immediate. Positivity of the real integral supplies the inequality used here and the integration of pointwise bounds. All these operations concern continuous functions on the same finite interval.

background_notes.fact: For tau>0, real beta!=0 and a continuously differentiable complex h on [0,tau], writing e(s)=exp(-i*beta*s), one has integral_0^tau h(s)e(s)ds=[h(s)e(s)/(-i*beta)]_0^tau-integral_0^tau h'(s)e(s)/(-i*beta)ds. Thus |tau^(-1) integral h*e| <= (|h(0)|+|h(tau)|+integral_0^tau |h'|)/(tau*|beta|).

Integrate the product derivative of h*e/(-i*beta) using the componentwise fundamental theorem of calculus to get the identity. Apply the triangle inequality, the continuous integral norm bound, |e|=1 and |-i*beta|=|beta|, then divide by positive tau.
